texts.1.1: Songs for CHILDREN by ISAAC WATTS, D. D. ILLUSTRATED
texts.1.2: PREFACE. TO ALL THAT ARE CONCERNED IN THE EDUCATION OF CHILDREN.
texts.2.1: It is an awful and important charge that is committed to you. The wisdom and welfare of the succeeding generation are intrusted with you before hand, and depend much on your conduct. The seeds of misery or happiness in this world, and that to come, are oftentimes sown very early; and, therefore, whatever may conduce to give the minds of children a relish for virtue and religion ought in the first place, to be proposed to you.
texts.2.2: Verse was at first designed for the service of God, though it hath been wretchedly abused since. The ancients among the Jews and the, Heathens taught their children and disciples the precepts of morality and worship in verse. The children of Israel were commanded to learn the words of the song of Moses, Deut. 31:19,30; and we are directed in the New Testament, not only to sing, "with grace in the heart," but to "teach and admonish one another by hymns and songs," Ephes. 5:19. And there are these four advantages in it: 1. There is a great delight in the very learning of truths and duties this way. There is something so amusing and entertaining in rhymes and metre that will incline children to make this part of their business a diversion. And you may turn their very duty into a reward, by giving them the privilege of learning one of these songs every week, if they fulfil the business of the week well, and promising them the book itself, when they have learned ten or twenty songs out of it. 2. What is learned in verse is longer retained in memory, and sooner recollected. The like sounds and the like number of syllables exceedingly assist the remembrance. And it may often happen that the end of a song, running in the mind, may be an effectual means to keep off some temptations, or to incline to some duty, when a word of scripture is not upon their thoughts. 3. This will be a constant furniture for the minds of children, that they may have something to think upon when alone, and sing over to themselves. This may sometimes give their thoughts a divine turn, and raise a young meditation. Thus they will not be forced to seek relief for an emptiness of mind out of the loose and dangerous sonnets of the age. 4. These Divine Songs may be a pleasant and proper matter for their daily or weekly worship, to sing one in the family at such time as the parents or governors shall appoint; and therefore I have confined the verse to the most usual psalm tunes.
texts.2.3: The greatest part of this little book was composed several years ago, at the request of a friend who has been long engaged in the work of catechising a very great number of children of all kinds, and with abundant skill and success, so that you will find here nothing that savours of a party: the children of high and low degree, of the Church of England or Dissenters, baptized in infancy or not, may all join together in these songs. And as I have endeavoured to sink the language to the level of a child's understanding and yet to keep it, if possible, above contempt, so I have designed to profit all, if possible, and offend none. I hope the more general the sense is, these composures may be of the more universal use and service.
texts.2.4: I have added at the end some attempts of sonnets on moral subjects, for children, with an air of pleasantry, to provoke some fitter pen to write a little book of them.
texts.2.5: May the Almighty God make you faithful in this important work of education: may he succeed your cares with his abundant grace; that the rising generation of Great Britain may be a glory among the nations, a pattern to the Christian world, and a blessing to the earth!
texts.2.8: Whatever opinion may be entertained by connoisseurs as to the value of Dr. Watts's Hymns as "Poems," none can doubt the earnest piety which dictated them, nor the unmistakable popularity they have ever enjoyed, both at home and abroad, and which fully entities them to be considered as genuine "Household Words".
texts.2.9: Numerous as are the editions already published, more or less illustrated, none have as yet approached the standard of completeness or excellence which such popularity deserves.
texts.2.10: The projectors of this effort fully believe that this want will be amply supplied by the production of the present edition. The names and number of the artists employed, together with the general care and finish bestowed throughout, they trust will be sufficient guarantee that their labour has not been in vain.
texts.2.11: It may be well to add that the whole of the Illustrations have been arranged and engraved under the entire direction of Mr. James D. Cooper.
texts.3.3: A General Song of Praise to God.
texts.3.5: How glorious is our heavenly King,
texts.3.7: How shall a child presume to sing

texts.3.10: Nor think how large his grace;
texts.3.11: Not men below, nor saints that dwell
texts.3.13: Not angels, that stand round the Lord,
texts.3.15: But they perform his heavenly word,
texts.3.17: Then let me join this holy train,
texts.3.19: Th' eternal God will not disdain
texts.3.21: My heart resolves, my tongue obeys;
texts.3.23: To hear their mighty Maker's praise
texts.3.28: I sing th' almighty power of God,
texts.3.30: That spread the flowing seas abroad,
texts.3.32: I sing the wisdom that ordain'd
texts.3.33: The sun to rule the day:
texts.3.34: The moon shines full at his command,

texts.3.37: That fill'd the earth with food:
texts.3.38: He form'd the creatures with his word,
texts.3.40: Lord, how thy wonders are display'd
texts.3.42: If I survey the ground I tread,

texts.3.46: And clouds arise and tempests blow,
texts.3.50: There's not a place where we can flee,
texts.3.52: In heaven he shines with beams of love,
texts.3.54: 'Tis on his earth I stand or move,
texts.3.55: And tis his air I breathe.
texts.3.56: His hand is my perpetual guard,
texts.3.57: He keeps me with his eye:
texts.3.58: Why should I then forget the Lord,
texts.3.61: Praise to God for our Redemption.
texts.3.63: Blest be the wisdom and the power,
texts.3.65: That join'd in counsel to restore
texts.3.69: And we, his children, thus were brought
texts.3.70: To death, and near to hell.
texts.3.71: Blest be the Lord, that sent his Son
texts.3.72: To take our flesh and blood!
texts.3.73: He for our lives gave up his own,
texts.3.74: To make our peace with God.
texts.3.75: He honour'd all his Father's laws,
texts.3.77: He bore our sins upon the cross,
texts.3.79: Behold him rising from the grave;
texts.3.81: He pleads his merits there, to save
texts.3.83: There, on a glorious throne, he reigns;
texts.3.85: Redeems us from the slavish chains
texts.3.87: Thence shall the Lord to judgment come;
texts.3.89: Shall call and break up every tomb,
texts.3.91: O may I then with joy appear
texts.3.93: And, with the blest assembly there,
texts.3.98: Whene'er I take my walks abroad,
texts.3.100: What shall I render to my God
texts.3.101: For all his gifts to me?
texts.3.102: Not more than others I deserve,
texts.3.103: Yet God hath given me more:
texts.3.104: For I have food, while others starve,
texts.3.105: Or beg from door to door.
texts.3.106: How many children in the street
texts.3.108: While I am clothed from head to feet,
texts.3.110: While some poor wretches scarce can tell
texts.3.111: Where they may lay their head,
texts.3.112: I have a home wherein to dwell,
texts.3.114: While others early learn to swear,
texts.3.115: And curse, and lie, and steal,
texts.3.116: Lord, I am taught thy name to fear,
texts.3.118: Are these thy favours, day by day,

texts.3.121: And try to serve thee best.
texts.3.123: Praise for birth and education in a Christian land.
texts.3.125: Great God, to thee my voice I raise,
texts.3.126: To thee my youngest hours belong:
texts.3.127: I would begin my life with praise,
texts.3.128: Till growing years improve the song.
texts.3.129: 'Tis to thy sovereign grace I owe
texts.3.130: That I was born on Christian ground;
texts.3.131: Where streams of heavenly mercy flow,
texts.3.132: And words of sweet salvation sound.

texts.3.136: Than east or western Indies hold.

texts.3.146: Since thou hast mark'd my way to heaven,
texts.3.147: Nor will I run the road to death,
texts.3.148: And waste the blessings thou hast given.

texts.3.153: And not to chance as others do,
texts.3.154: That I was born of Christian race,

texts.4.103: They wear not their time out in sleeping or play,
texts.4.104: But gather up corn in a sunshiny day,
texts.4.105: And for winter they lay up their stores:
texts.4.106: They manage their work in such regular forms,
texts.4.107: One would think they foresaw all the frosts and the storms,
texts.4.108: And so brought their food withindoors.
texts.4.109: But I have less sense than a poor creeping Ant,
texts.4.110: If I take not due care for the things I shall want,
texts.4.111: Nor provide against dangers in time;
texts.4.112: When death or old age shall once stare in my face,
texts.4.113: What a wretch shall I be in the end of my days,
texts.4.114: If I trifle away all their prime!
texts.4.115: Now, now, while my strength and my youth are in bloom,
texts.4.116: Let me think what shall serve me when sickness shall come,
texts.4.117: And pray that my sins be forgiven.
texts.4.118: Let me read in good books, and believe, and obey;
texts.4.119: That, when death turns me out of this cottage of clay,
texts.4.120: I may dwell in a palace in heaven.
texts.4.124: Though I'm now in younger days,
texts.4.125: Nor can tell what shall befall me,
texts.4.127: Where my growing age shall call me.
texts.4.128: Should I e'er be rich or great,
texts.4.130: I'll supply the poor with meat,
texts.4.132: Where I see the blind or lame,
texts.4.133: Deaf or dumb, I'll kindly treat them:
texts.4.134: I deserve to feel the same,
texts.4.135: I I mock, or hurt, or cheat them.
texts.4.136: If I meet with railing tongues,
texts.4.137: Why should I return them railing,
texts.4.138: Since I best revenge my wrongs
texts.4.140: When I hear them telling lies,
texts.4.142: First I'll try to make them wise,
texts.4.143: Or I'll soon go out of hearing.
texts.4.144: What though I be low or mean,
texts.4.145: I'll engage the rich to love me,
texts.4.146: While I'm modest, neat, and clean,
texts.4.147: And submit when they reprove me.
texts.4.148: If I should be poor and sick,
texts.4.149: I shall meet, I hope, with pity;
texts.4.150: Since I love to help the weak,
texts.4.151: Though they're neither fair nor witty.
texts.4.154: What's amiss I'll strive to mend,
texts.4.155: And endure what can't be mended.
texts.4.156: May I be so watchful still
texts.4.157: O'er my humours and my passion,
texts.4.158: As to speak and do no ill,
texts.4.159: Though it should be all the fashion.
texts.4.161: Ne'er may I be found complying;
texts.4.162: But in life behave so well,
texts.4.163: Not to be afraid of dying.
texts.4.167: How fine has the day been! how bright was the sun!
texts.4.168: How lovely and joyful the course that he run;
texts.4.169: Though he rose in a mist when his race he begun,
texts.4.170: And there followed some droppings of rain:
texts.4.171: But now the fair traveller's come to the west,
texts.4.172: His rays are all gold, and his beauties are best;
texts.4.173: He paints the skies gay as he sinks to his rest,
texts.4.174: And foretells a bright rising again.
texts.4.175: Just such is the Christian. His course he begins
texts.4.176: Like the sun in a mist, while he mourns for his sins,
texts.4.177: And melts into tears! then he breaks out and shines,
texts.4.179: But when he comes nearer to finish his race,
texts.4.180: Like a fine setting sun, he looks richer in grace;
texts.4.181: And gives a sure hope, at the end of his days,
texts.4.185: Hush, my dear! Lie still, and slumber!
texts.4.189: Sleep, my babe! thy food and raiment,
texts.4.190: House and home, thy friends provide;
texts.4.191: All without thy care or payment,
texts.4.192: All thy wants are well supplied.
texts.4.194: Than the Son of God could be,
texts.4.196: And became a child like thee!
texts.4.197: Soft and easy is thy cradle:
texts.4.198: Coarse and hard thy Saviour lay,
texts.4.199: When his birthplace was a stable,
texts.4.200: And his softest bed was hay.
texts.4.203: Must he dwell with brutal creatures?
texts.4.204: How could angels bear the sight?
texts.4.205: Was there nothing but a manger
texts.4.208: Did they thus affront the Lord?
texts.4.209: Soft, my child! I did not chide thee,
texts.4.210: Though my song might sound too hard:
texts.4.212: And her arm shall be thy guard.
texts.4.213: Yet to read the shameful story.
texts.4.214: How the Jews received their King,
texts.4.215: How they served the Lord of Glory,
texts.4.216: Makes me angry while I sing.
texts.4.217: See the kinder shepherds round him,
texts.4.219: Where hey sought him, there they found him,
texts.4.223: When he wept, his mother's blessing
texts.4.224: Sooth'd and hush'd the holy Child.
texts.4.225: Lo, he slumbers in a manger,
texts.4.227: Peace, my darling, here's no danger:
texts.4.228: There's no ox a-near thy bed.
texts.4.229: 'Twas so save thee, child, from dying,
texts.4.230: Save my dear from burning flame,
texts.4.233: May'st thou live to know and fear him,
texts.4.234: Trust and love him all thy days,
texts.4.235: Then go dwell for ever near him:
texts.4.236: See his face, and sing his praise!
texts.4.237: I could give thee thousand kisses!
